title: In 1946 a Japanese abacus beat an electric calculator 4 to 1

cover.alt: A wooden Japanese soroban with rows of dark beads on thin rods, one bead above the beam and four below on each rod.

body: On 11 November 1946 in Tokyo, Kiyoshi Matsuzaki with a **soroban** faced US Army Private Thomas Nathan Wood with an electric calculator, in a contest of speed and accuracy in addition, subtraction, multiplication and division plus one combined problem. The beads won 4 to 1; the machine only took multiplication. A soroban works because each rod holds a single digit: one bead above the beam is worth five and the four below are worth one each, so a trained user's fingers carry out the arithmetic almost without thinking. Skilled users go further and calculate with an imagined soroban, a practice called *anzan*.

slides.prompt: The contest had five rounds. Which was the only one the electric calculator won?
slides.detail: The abacus took both addition heats, won subtraction and division two heats to one, and won the composite problem. The calculator won only multiplication, two heats to one.

slides.heading: Rounds won in the 1946 Tokyo contest
slides.note: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and a combined problem, 11 November 1946

slides.heading: How one rod holds a digit
items: One bead above the beam counts five
Four beads below count one each
Beads pushed to the beam are "on"
Seven is one upper bead plus two lower

slides.heading: From China to Japan
slides.text: The soroban descends from the Chinese suanpan, which reached Japan after the mid 15th century. Its one-above, four-below layout was created in 1891, when Irie Garyū removed one bead from each rod, and it became popular in the 1940s. A soroban always has an odd number of rods, never fewer than seven.

slides.heading: Still taught today
slides.text: Japanese elementary schools are no longer required to teach the soroban, but many children learn it in private after-school classes. The Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry runs a six-level certification exam, and advanced students practise anzan: calculating on a soroban they only picture in their heads.

slides.question: Why is a soroban so fast in trained hands?
options: Each rod is one digit, moved by reflex
slides.explanation: Every rod is one decimal digit, with a five-bead above the beam and four one-beads below, so a practised user's fingers run the arithmetic almost automatically.
